newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia seeks financial boon from tsarist debt deal.
newsitem.headline: Russia seeks financial boon from tsarist debt deal.

text.p: Russia's agreement with France to repay part of Moscow's tsarist-era debt signals its desire to win international financial respectability -- in stark contrast to the economic mess at home.

The deal will repay around $400 million, a fraction of the $30 billion or so claimed by French bondholders. Analysts said it was part of Russia's efforts to ensure its creditworthiness as its need to tap international markets becomes more acute.
"Full international creditworthiness is one of the best hopes for getting over a very difficult problem in the domestic economy," said Christopher Granville, head of research at United City Bank.
"Domestic interest rates are still far too high so if they can tap international markets, this could be the way through."

The debt deal, reached at Paris talks between Prime Ministers Viktor Chernomyrdin and Alain Juppe required Moscow to pay $400 million to some 400,000 holders of the bonds, which were issued before the 1917 Bolshevik revolution.

"I imagine repayments would be very small in the first few years and more later, which means the pressure on the budget in the next two to three years will be very limited," said Renaissance Capital chief economist Roland Nash.
The Soviet government repudiated the debt, but ministers have stressed Russia will meet its obligations, however ancient.
Russia has already reached agreements with the Paris and London Clubs of sovereign and commercial bank creditors to reschedule debts inherited from the Soviet Union.
These deals were a pre-condition to Moscow's $10 billion loan from the International Monetary Fund agreed in March.
Russia is keen to join the Paris Club as a creditor in order to get a share of the billions of dollars owed to the Soviet Union, mostly by developing countries.
"The tsarist debt was a sore point among several members of the Paris Club, especially France, and making this token gesture does advance this process quite a long way," said Nash.

Russia has already taken major steps towards financial rehabilitation, crowning this last Thursday when, after receiving a good speculative credit rating, it issued a $1 billion bond, which was oversubscribed.
But economic problems remain.
The IMF has delayed payment of the latest part of its loan because of persistent concern over low tax collection.
And the communist-dominated State Duma lower house of parliament has rejected the 1997 budget which could make it harder for the IMF to pay up next year.

Officials are looking into a scandal involving dollar-denominated finance ministry bonds which were frozen in June. The ministry said the bonds would be unfrozen if the securities had been acquired in good faith.
Furthermore, the revenue shortfall has led to a build up of non-payments and many workers have not been paid for months. Wage arrears were 43 trillion rubles ($7.8 billion) on Oct. 28.
"As a Russian colleague said, it seems very strange that they are willing to take on this (tsarist) debt when they are not even paying wages," said Nash.
Nash said the government had not been obliged to take on the tsarist debt and that some investors might be surprised.
"They have put their fiscal house back in order and now they are going around adopting unnecessary debt," he said.
